clue.text: Dicing with communism turned out to be Corbyn's worst nightmare

indicators.note: something that turned out differently has been reshaped, so the letters of the two words are rearranged

explanation.surface: Playing games with communism proved a disaster for the former Labour leader.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turned out' rearranges DICING and COMMUNISM together into the name of Boris Johnson's chief adviser.
explanation.definitionFit: The Vote Leave strategist who ran Johnson's 2019 campaign helped deliver Labour's heavy defeat under Jeremy Corbyn.

clue.text: Odd bod Major in the frame?

indicators.note: odd here means strange or out of order, so the letters of the next two words are rearranged

explanation.surface: A strange chap called Major is under suspicion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Odd' looks like part of the phrase 'odd bod' (a peculiar person) but it signals rearranging BOD and MAJOR. The definition plays on 'in the frame', meaning suspected, versus literally part of a door frame.
explanation.definitionFit: The vertical post at the side of a doorway is one component of the door's surround.

clue.text: Furs ordered by flirtatious girl

parts.note: the pelts a coquette might ask for, with the joke that a flirt is called a minx, which is said exactly like the fur animals' plural

explanation.surface: A coquettish young woman puts in an order for fur coats.
explanation.walkthrough: A whole-clue cryptic definition: a flirtatious girl is a minx, and the furs she orders share that sound.
explanation.definitionFit: These are coats or pelts from small semi-aquatic weasel-like animals farmed for luxury fur.

clue.text: Nothing new (9)

parts.note: nine in Roman numerals is IX

explanation.surface: Nothing fresh to report, as if pointing to clue 9.
explanation.walkthrough: The bracketed (9) looks like a cross-reference to 9 Across, but it is simply the number nine, written IX in Roman numerals.
explanation.definitionFit: A slang word meaning zero or nil, also used as a verb for refusing or cancelling.

clue.text: Bring up the field, Brian is batting

parts.note: Brian Close was a Yorkshire and England cricket captain
in cricket the side or player batting is said to be in

explanation.surface: A cricket captain moves his fielders up while Brian takes his turn at the crease.
explanation.definitionFit: Fielders are said to come nearer the batsman to apply pressure; the phrase is to move nearer or encircle.

clue.text: Parcel delivery firm to press for a huge rise

parts.note: UPS is the United Parcel Service
to press for something is to urge it

explanation.surface: A courier company campaigns for a big pay increase.
explanation.definitionFit: A sudden large increase or surge in amount, such as a boom in sales or support.

clue.text: Liverpool striker nursing the onset of gum disease

indicators.note: nursing means holding or cradling, so the striker's name holds a letter inside it

parts.note: Sadio Mane was a Liverpool forward

indicators.note: the onset is the start, so only the first letter of gum is used

explanation.surface: A footballer is treating early signs of gum disease.
explanation.walkthrough: 'nursing' puts G, from 'the onset of gum', inside MANE. 'gum disease' looks like one phrase but 'disease' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A skin condition of animals caused by parasitic mites, giving hair loss and itching.

clue.text: Butt/cask knocked over

indicators.note: something knocked over is upended, so in a down clue the word is turned the other way

parts.note: a tun is a large cask for wine or beer

explanation.surface: A barrel, or butt, gets tipped over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'knocked over' turns TUN round. 'Butt' and 'cask' look like synonyms, since a butt is also a cask, but 'Butt' is the verb meaning to strike with the head.
explanation.definitionFit: To strike with the head, as in a headbutt, which is slang for this blow.

clue.text: Small shelf on which to put slipper?

parts.note: a ledge is a narrow shelf

explanation.surface: A little shelf to keep your house slippers on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'slipper' is not footwear but one who slips or slides, and this is what they ride on over snow.
explanation.definitionFit: A sled carries a person gliding over snow and ice, playfully called a slipper.

clue.text: Horrid old boy, Oscar, American, outside no.11

indicators.note: outside here means placed beyond, so the last pieces sit after the number

parts.note: no. abbreviates number, and eleven is XI in Roman numerals
Oscar is O in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A nasty former pupil, an American called Oscar, hangs about outside number 11.
explanation.walkthrough: 'outside' places OUS after NOXI rather than around it.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe someone extremely unpleasant or offensive in manner.

clue.text: Gammon I treated, infused by saltpetre

indicators.note: a thing infused by something has it soaked right through, so the answer lies within these words

explanation.surface: Ham cured with saltpetre, as in traditional curing.
explanation.definitionFit: Potassium nitrate, also called saltpetre, used in curing meat and in gunpowder.

clue.text: Breaking news: English politician in government stepping down at next election

definitions.text: politician in government stepping down at next election

parts.note: news just announced is described as just in
a Green is a member of the Green Party

explanation.surface: Headline news: a minister announces she will not stand again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'politician' and 'in government' serve twice in the surface, but each word does one job: GREEN, IN and G build the surname.
explanation.definitionFit: The former Conservative education secretary announced in 2019 she would not contest her Putney seat.

clue.text: Deduce a terrible fire? No, no

indicators.note: No here means without or minus, so the next word is removed

parts.note: an inferno is a huge destructive blaze
taken as written, the two letters to drop

explanation.surface: Someone guesses a blaze is raging, and is told firmly it isn't.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No, no' reads as emphatic denial, but means 'no NO': INFERNO without NO.
explanation.definitionFit: To reach a conclusion by reasoning from evidence, the same sense as reasoning something out.

clue.text: Run into … into bars at the opening

indicators.note: into means placed inside, so the letter goes inside the following word

parts.note: R is the cricket abbreviation for run

explanation.surface: A stuttering phrase about running into bars at opening time.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue says it literally: 'Run into into', R placed inside INTO.
explanation.definitionFit: The opening few bars of a song or piece of music, the short introductory passage.

clue.text: Order mortifying neat, honourable gentleman

indicators.note: to order is to arrange, so the letters of the two following words are put in a new sequence

explanation.surface: The Speaker's call of 'Order!' mortifies a tidy MP.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Order' rearranges MORTIFYING and NEAT; 'honourable gentleman' is how MPs address one another in the Commons.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone honest and principled, which an honourable person is supposed to be.

clue.text: He's good at serving eggs in Norfolk on vacation

indicators.note: in means placed inside, so the eggs go into the remaining letters
a place on vacation is emptied, so its middle letters go, leaving its outer pair

parts.note: ova is the Latin plural for eggs

explanation.surface: A cook serves eggs while holidaying in Norfolk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on vacation' empties Norfolk to NK; 'serving' suggests food but means serving at tennis.
explanation.definitionFit: First name of the Serbian tennis champion Djokovic, a player with a formidable serve.

clue.text: Managed to admit party element "somewhat toxic"

indicators.note: to admit is to let in, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: ran means managed, as in ran a business
a do is a party

explanation.surface: Someone ran a party that was called slightly poisonous.
explanation.walkthrough: 'somewhat toxic' is wry understatement for a radioactive gas.
explanation.definitionFit: A radioactive noble gas, a chemical element that seeps from rocks and is a health hazard.

clue.text: Phoning in sick, I call foul — like the business of Boris bikes?

definitions.text: like the business of Boris bikes?

indicators.note: phoning in means speaking on the telephone, so the words are heard rather than read
foul signals a poor rendition, the words slurred together to make a new word

parts.note: the three words spoken quickly

explanation.surface: Calling in sick, I cry foul, a jibe about London's cycle hire scheme.
explanation.walkthrough: Spoken together, 'sick, I call' run into the answer. Boris bikes are London's hire bicycles, named after Boris Johnson as mayor.
explanation.definitionFit: Going round in recurring rounds, as an economy does, and also a punning nod to cycling.

clue.text: Absolutely no place for the Edstone, said Miliband

definitions.meaning: an emphatic refusal, never while I live

definitions.text: place for the Edstone, said Miliband
definitions.meaning: Ed Miliband's 2015 stone tablet of pledges, mocked as a headstone, would stand above his corpse

explanation.surface: Miliband insists his stone tablet of pledges has nowhere to go.
explanation.walkthrough: The Edstone was a giant engraved slab of Labour election promises in 2015, widely mocked as a tombstone.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom is an emphatic refusal; literally, a grave marker sits above a buried body.

clue.text: American woodpeckers regularly nicking bits of your cake (and The Queen's!)

indicators.note: taking bits at regular intervals means picking every other letter of each word

parts.note: ER is the Queen, Elizabeth Regina, and the possessive adds S

explanation.surface: Birds pecking crumbs from your cake, and the monarch's too.
explanation.definitionFit: A North American folk name for the flicker, a type of woodpecker, given in the plural.

clue.text: Dump former partner on holiday island in The Med

parts.note: an ex is a former spouse or partner
Crete is a popular Greek island in the Mediterranean

explanation.surface: Someone abandons their ex while holidaying in Crete.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dump' suggests ditching a partner, but it is the crude sense of expelling waste.
explanation.definitionFit: To discharge waste from the body; dump is a slang verb for defecating.

clue.text: Son, very French, beginning to suffer tension

parts.note: tres is French for very

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: A son, terribly French, starts to suffer from nerves.
explanation.definitionFit: Strain or pressure, mental or physical, is the sense shared by both words.

clue.text: Withdraw offensive Tory poster, having left off 1A's slogan

parts.note: to withdraw a remark is to take it back

indicators.note: having goes with off, the pair saying a letter has been taken away
off here means removed, so one letter is dropped

parts.note: a Tory is a Con, and a troll is someone who posts offensive messages online

explanation.surface: Pull a nasty Conservative billboard, having dropped the adviser's catchphrase.
explanation.walkthrough: 'poster' suggests a billboard but means someone who posts online. 'having left off' drops one L from CONTROLL.
explanation.definitionFit: The Vote Leave campaign motto of 2016 was devised by Dominic Cummings, the solution at 1 Across.

clue.text: Upending a huge chunk of wood

indicators.note: upending turns something upside down, so in a down entry the letters run the other way

parts.note: a slab is a big thick piece

explanation.surface: Tipping over a big block of timber.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Upending' reverses A SLAB; 'chunk of wood' looks like the definition, but 'wood' alone is.
explanation.definitionFit: A very light tropical timber used for model-making and rafts.

clue.text: Gag when rolling cheroot, blowing rings

indicators.note: rolling tobacco mixes it up, so the remaining letters are rearranged
blowing smoke rings sends them away, so those letters are dropped

parts.note: rings are O shapes, two of them

explanation.surface: A smoker heaves while rolling a cigar and blowing smoke rings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'blowing rings' removes two Os from CHEROOT, leaving CHERT, and 'rolling' rearranges that.
explanation.definitionFit: To gag is to heave as if about to vomit.

clue.text: Echo Neeson's revolting message?

parts.note: Echo is E in the NATO phonetic alphabet

indicators.note: revolting means turning over, so the first name is turned backwards

parts.note: Liam Neeson is a Northern Irish actor

explanation.surface: An actor's disgusting reply, repeated back to him.
explanation.walkthrough: 'revolting' looks like disgust, but signals the name reversed.
explanation.definitionFit: An electronic message sent between computers, the commonest kind of written note today.

clue.text: First-class resistance song

parts.note: A1 means first-class, written here as AI
R is the symbol for electrical resistance

explanation.surface: A superb protest anthem.
explanation.definitionFit: A tune or melody, as in Bach's famous piece for strings on the G string.

clue.text: Very active base, new group run by Rees-Mogg to call back

parts.note: e is the base of natural logarithms
the ERG, European Research Group, was the Eurosceptic Tory caucus chaired by Jacob Rees-Mogg

indicators.note: back means turned round, so the word is read in reverse

parts.note: to cite is to call, as a witness is cited

explanation.surface: A lively base for a new pressure group, led by Rees-Mogg, calling for return.
explanation.definitionFit: Full of vigour and energy, a lively person being highly active.

clue.text: Contemptible person, guilty at regular intervals

indicators.note: letters taken at regular intervals are every other one, starting with the first

explanation.surface: A despicable person, guilty now and again.
explanation.definitionFit: A British slang insult for an unpleasant or foolish person.

clue.text: Second page: the leadership bullied the ex-Chancellor

indicators.note: bullied means knocked about, so the letters are thrown into a new order

explanation.surface: On page two: the party leadership pushed around the former Chancellor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bullied' rearranges THE LEADERSHIP. The nickname mocked Philip Hammond, Chancellor of the Exchequer (finance minister) until 2019, for his dry, numbers-first manner.
explanation.definitionFit: This was the nickname of Philip Hammond, who held the Treasury's top job until 2019.
